The WHO clinical guidelines address the care of children and adolescents (aged 0–18 years) who have been or may have been exposed to sexual abuse. Additionally, the guidelines examine whether screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are more effective than presumptive treatment in preventing and managing adverse outcomes, such as emotional and behavioral disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and caregiver outcomes like stress and stigma. The guidelines also address topics for which existing WHO recommendations were used, including pregnancy prevention and management (e.g., emergency contraception and safe abortion), vaccines to prevent STIs (e.g., hepatitis B and human papillomavirus), HIV prevention (e.g., PEP regimens), and mental health interventions for emotional and behavioral disorders. Good clinical practices are outlined for childand adolescent-centered, gender-sensitive, and trauma-informed care. These include principles for obtaining medical history, conducting forensic interviews, performing physical examinations, and minimizing harm or trauma during forensic investigations. Recommendations are also provided for documenting medical history and examination findings, as well as for reporting requirements in the context of laws on sexual consent or statutory rape. The values and preferences of healthcare providers, institutions, children, adolescents, and their caregivers regarding the reporting of sexual abuse are also considered. The guidelines emphasize ethical, safety, and human rights principles in clinical practice. They also highlight good practices for providing information and education about sexual abuse to children, adolescents, and their caregivers to promote timely access to health services.
